---
title: "First measured results (provisional)"
---

> **Provisional.** These are first results from two automated runs of the
> package's default pipeline (21 and 22 November 2026 UTC) and one live test
> run (22 November 2026 UTC), on CDC AtlasPlus data as returned on those
> dates. They cover HIV prevalence (people living with diagnosed HIV), ages 13
> and older, for 2017, 2022 and 2024, with default settings. They have not
> been independently checked. The defaults they describe may change. Fuller
> articles with figures will replace this page.

This page reports what the package's steps did to real data: how much CDC
suppresses, what `impute_suppressed()` fills in, and what is left over. It has
no code that downloads data. For what CDC's numbers mean, see
[About CDC AtlasPlus data](about-atlasplus-data.html); for the tract
estimates, see [Extrapolation to tracts](extrapolation.html).

Every number produced by `impute_suppressed()` is a modeled estimate, not a
count CDC withheld. Nothing here says how large any suppressed count is.

## How much CDC suppresses at county level

The more finely the data are divided, the more county rows are suppressed.

| Share of county rows suppressed | 2017 | 2022 | 2024 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Not stratified | 15% | 14% | 13% |
| By sex | 44% | 43% | 42% |
| By age | 50% | 49% | 48% |
| By race | 60% | 58% | 57% |

## What the default imputation does

By default, `impute_suppressed()` estimates a suppressed county row as the
state's rate times the county's population, and caps the estimate at 4. In
2022 the cap, not the state rate, set most of the estimates, except by race.

| 2022 | Not stratified | By sex | By age | By race |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Estimates above 4 before the cap | 77% | 71% | 50% | 15% |
| Cases the cap takes off the estimated total | 3,807 | 56,020 | 58,857 | 30,927 |

These are facts about the estimates. An estimate above 4 does not show that
the hidden count is above 4. The column `cases_uncapped` lets you count the
same thing for your own request.

Changing the settings moved the 2022 national total of published and
estimated county cases by this much:

| Setting | Not stratified | By sex |
|---|---|---|
| `method = "zero"` | −0.15% | −0.90% |
| `cap = Inf` | +0.35% | +5.28% |
| `floor = 1` | under 0.01% | under 0.01% |
| `population = "acs"` | under 0.01% | under 0.01% |

## Stratified estimates against the county's own total

A county's count is often published while some of its counts by sex, age or
race are suppressed. Adding up such a county's strata, published and
estimated, should give about the county's published count. Under the default
it often does not.

| 2022 | By sex | By age | By race |
|---|---|---|---|
| Counties whose strata sum to under 90% of their count | 717 | 388 | 273 |
| Counties whose strata sum to over 110% of their count | 112 | 815 | 386 |
| Cases short, added over counties | 22,763 | 21,241 | 17,590 |
| Cases over, added over counties | 313 | 5,528 | 2,479 |

So stratified estimates under the default do not add up to the unstratified
ones. By sex they fall short. By age they fall short in some counties and run
over in others.

The comparison uses counties whose unstratified count is published; the 90%
and 110% rows need that count to be above zero. Counties with exactly one
suppressed stratum cell are left out. By race, a county can fall short with
no suppressed stratum at all, because CDC puts cases of unknown race in no
row.

## Cases in state totals but in no county row

`no_county_cases()` reports each state's total minus its published county
counts minus the estimates for its suppressed counties. Added over states
(shortfalls and excesses offset each other), after the default imputation:

| | 2017 | 2022 | 2024 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sum of state totals | 1,002,796 | 1,102,798 | 1,157,995 |
| Remainder, not stratified | 33,025 | 20,028 | 17,530 |
| Remainder, by sex | 51,988 | 41,696 | 40,514 |
| Remainder, by age | 39,541 | 33,238 | 34,698 |
| Remainder, by race | 44,429 | 33,659 | 32,382 |

In a few states the remainder was a large share of the state's total in 2022:

| 2022 | States and share of the state's total |
|---|---|
| Not stratified | Alaska 87%, Rhode Island 73%, Nebraska 60%, Idaho 47%, Vermont 19%, Wyoming 14% |
| By sex | New Hampshire 94%, Maine 93%, Idaho 81%, Alaska 81%, Rhode Island 74% |

This is consistent with those states' county counts being largely suppressed.
The cause has not been verified. County or tract estimates for such a state
leave most of its cases out. `no_county_cases()` and
`extrapolate_from_county()` now warn when more than 25% of a state's cases
are in no county row, and name the states with their shares.

## What CDC's data look like inside a county

These come from the live test run, which recorded counts only, for HIV
diagnoses and HIV prevalence.

Where every stratum of a county is published, the strata sum exactly to the
county's count by sex and by age, in every year checked. By race, diagnoses
also sum exactly, but prevalence sums to less in about a fifth of such
counties and never to more. That is consistent with unknown race being in no
row.

| Prevalence by race, counties with every stratum published | 2017 | 2022 | 2024 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Counties | 233 | 244 | 244 |
| Strata sum to less than the county's count | 47 | 51 | 54 |

Counties with a published count and exactly one suppressed stratum cell are
rare. There were none in 2022, 2024 or 2025, for either indicator, by sex,
age or race. In 2017 there were a few: 1 for diagnoses by age, 2 for
diagnoses by race and 5 for prevalence by race.

## What this means for users now

- **Unstratified estimates.** Nationally, county and tract estimates changed
  little with the imputation settings. That does not hold in the states
  listed above, where most cases are in no county row.
- **Estimates by sex, age or race.** Under the default, about 3% to 4% of
  national cases in 2022 were in no county row, against about 2% without
  stratification, and far more in some states and counties.
- **Report your settings.** Say which `method`, `cap`, `floor` and
  `population` you used, and consider running the alternatives above as
  sensitivity analyses.
- **A better method is being designed.** It will fit stratified estimates to
  each county's published total. Until then, treat stratified estimates for
  counties with suppressed strata with caution.
- **Race denominators need a closer look.** Census and CDC populations by
  race can differ for the same county; this has not yet been measured
  carefully enough to report.
